cost/ask: Before training a model, you want to know how long the run will take. An hour, or a month? It pays to work out the bill first.
cost/gpu: Training runs on GPUs, short for graphics processing units: chips first built to draw graphics, which do thousands of multiplications at once.
cost/alex: In 2012, the authors of AlexNet wrote that its size was limited by their GPUs' memory, and by the training time they were willing to tolerate: between five and six days, on two GPUs.
cost/flop: Floating point is how a computer stores a decimal, like three point one four. One multiply or one add of two such numbers is one floating point operation: a FLOP.
cost/plan: A GPU's speed is counted in FLOPs per second. Divide the FLOPs a run needs by that speed, and out comes the time. So count the FLOPs.
forward/layer: Count one layer. W holds twelve weights, and x is the vector for one token passing through.
forward/mult: Each weight multiplies one entry of x, and the product joins a running sum. Row one: three times two, plus one times one, plus zero times three, plus two times one: nine.
forward/mark: Tally what each weight cost: one multiply, and one add into the sum. Two FLOPs per weight, for every token.
forward/n: Write N for the number of parameters, a different N from the count of blocks before. Here N is twelve, so one token costs twenty four FLOPs: two N.
backward/back: Training then runs backprop through the same layer, and backprop needs two more products, each as big as the forward one.
backward/dx: W transpose, d z passes the gradient back to x, for the layer below. It uses every weight once more, in a multiply and an add: two more FLOPs.
backward/dW: Then each weight gets its own gradient. The weight in row i, column j gets d z entry i, times x entry j: one multiply.
backward/acc: Training reads many tokens, and each token's product is added into the weight's running gradient: one add.
backward/six: Two forward and four backward: six FLOPs per parameter, for every token.
backward/kaplan: Jared Kaplan and colleagues estimated training this way in 2020: the backward pass costs about twice the forward, so about six FLOPs per parameter per token, leaving out smaller costs.
backward/d: Write D for the number of tokens the model trains on, counting repeats.
backward/c: Every parameter works on every token, so the run costs six, times N, times D: six N D FLOPs. Call it C, the training compute.
run/model: Now a real run: a model of three billion parameters, trained on forty billion tokens.
run/lead: Multiply the leading numbers: six times three times four is seventy two.
run/pow: Multiplying powers of ten adds them: ten to the nine, times ten to the ten, is ten to the nineteen. So seventy two times ten to the nineteen FLOPs.
run/shift: Seventy two is seven point two times ten, so move the decimal point one place, and the power grows by one: seven point two times ten to the twenty.
run/same: Only the product of N and D matters. Twice the parameters on half the tokens would cost exactly the same.
run/rate: Say one GPU sustains two times ten to the fourteen FLOPs per second. A hundred of them together do two times ten to the sixteen.
run/div: Divide the leading numbers: seven point two over two is three point six.
run/sub: Dividing powers of ten subtracts them: twenty minus sixteen is four. So three point six times ten to the four seconds: thirty six thousand.
run/hours: An hour is three thousand six hundred seconds, so the run takes ten hours.
run/fwd: Once it is trained, each token it reads takes the forward pass alone: two N, six billion FLOPs, a third of what training on it cost.
